newsitem.title: USA: Iraq may be allowed only limited oil sales overrun.
newsitem.headline: Iraq may be allowed only limited oil sales overrun.

text.p: Iraq may be allowed to carry over only five percent of its $1 billion quarterly limit for oil sales under its "oil-for-food" deal with the United Nations, Western diplomats said on Tuesday.

The requirement would mean Iraq, having delayed for two months the restart of oil exports, will have to sell oil at a much higher rate in August than was previously reckoned, or forego some of its oil sales under the scheme.

"It is $1 billion for 90 days, the resolution is clear. There is around five percent (overrun) allowed for technical reasons but not 45 percent," said a Western diplomat on the U.N. Iraq sanctions committee.
"Five percent is all that is allowed. It would require another (U.N. Security Council) resolution to change it," said another senior diplomat, also on the sanctions panel.
A U.N. official involved in administering the deal said the overrun is the subject of debate currently.
"The basic documents say only $1 billion in a 90-day period and it is up to the sanctions committee interpretation whether overruns are allowed," the U.N. official said.

"Overruns were allowed in the first 90 days because of various technicalities in administering new contracts and so on. But when it regards a potentially significantly larger amount, they may not allow it," he added.

Iraq was allowed by a U.N. resolution taking effect June 8 to renew its deal to sell $2 billion of oil for humanitarian aid, in two $1 billion increments every 90 days. Iraq sold about 660,000 barrels per day (bpd) from December 10, 1996 to June 7, 1997.

The renewed oil sales have been stalled, however, pending agreement on a new aid distribution plan. The plan is expected to be passed to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annon for final approval early next week, U.N. officials said.
A new oil price formula and individual contracts with oil companies must then be approved by the U.N.-appointed overseers in New York.

This is expected to take only a matter of days, but a potential hitch has arisen with the illness of the U.S. overseer, former Exxon Corp executive Maurice Lorenz, who recently suffered a mild stroke, diplomats said.

The remaining two overseers are from France and Russia. Oil contracts must be signed by two overseers which are not nationals of the country of the oil buyer and as Iraq is expected to renew or even increase contracts with French and Russian companies, a replacement would have to be found if Lorenz cannot return to work, possibly causing a short delay.

Assuming oil sales don't begin again until the last week of July, at the earliest, Iraq would then have about 40 days in which to sell around $1 billion of oil, or more than 1.5 million bpd at current prices unless the rules are altered, diplomats said.

Iraq's oil minister at the end of June estimated that oil sales would restart at a rate of about 750,000 bpd in early July and the oil industry has expected the $2 billion sales to be smoothed out over 180 days.

"Technically, they can do it. But from a marketing point of view people will be very reluctant to take that much oil in August," said a trader for an oil company which had a contract to lift oil in the first round.
The sanctions panel view appears to be fairly firmly against allowing Iraq too much leeway in carrying over oil sales into the second 90 day period.
"If Iraq took two months hanging around, dithering about the aid plan, that's really nothing to do with us," said a senior Western diplomat.
